A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite reflow; v3 adds theoretical material and Appendix L.

before.justification: v2 reports original CLEVR experiments and manual counts in Table 1, SDXL compositions, CLIP analyses, and synthetic sampling experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds explicit-composition experiments and score diagnostics in Appendix L. The learned-composition baseline results are separately attributed to Bradley (2025).

M1.justification: The core composition operator remains unchanged. Appendix L adds a learned-background variant using an empty conditioner and an inference variant that switches from learned to unconditional background after 12 denoising steps.

E1.justification: CLEVR remains the experimental domain, but Appendix L adds all-object location/color conditioning, empty out-of-distribution conditioners, and multi-color length-generalization tests. Earlier CLEVR color experiments primarily composed pairs of single-color distributions.

E2.justification: Beyond v2's comparisons among explicit compositions, v3 directly compares them with Bradley (2025)'s learned single-model composition in Table 2. Learned and switching backgrounds also join the empty and unconditional background comparisons.

E3.justification: Appendix L introduces a separate evaluation across training ranges from one object through 1–6 objects, using maximum successful composition size Kmax. Figures 17–18 add score comparisons across denoising times and clean-image conditioning controls. The earlier 100-image manual-count protocol remains unchanged; Table 2 refers externally for its precise success criterion.

E4.justification: Appendix L adds background and training-range analyses, including a background-switch intervention. Figures 17–18 examine when learned, explicit, and unconditional scores agree, providing new evidence about denoising mechanisms beyond the retained composition and sampling analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained count histograms and newly added score trajectories do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Earlier numerical and visual results, including Table 1, are retained. New Table 2 reports, for training on 1–3 objects, Kmax values of 9 for learned composition, 8 for explicit composition with learned background, and 4 with empty background. Figures 16–18 add color-composition failures and score-agreement findings under new settings.

T1.justification: v3 adds Lemma 5.7 and an Appendix H derivation claiming a bound KL(C*||C) <= epsilon_b + sum_i epsilon_i under partially relaxed independence assumptions. This substantially extends the stated distribution-level theory beyond exact factorization; the existing sampling guarantees are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, Section 1.1 contribution statement, and conclusion preserve the same main claims about projective composition, sufficient conditions, feature-space composition, sampling limitations, and the practical heuristic.

C2.justification: Appendix L introduces a mechanism combining high-noise compositional structure with low-noise local unconditional denoising. It also discusses crowding, composition of object clusters, and learned feature transformations to explain differences between learned and explicit composition, extending v2's interpretations substantially.

D1.justification: Appendix L documents a 16×16 location-count representation, eight-component color conditioning, exact test locations and colors, and background construction and switching details. Earlier implementation disclosures remain unchanged; the new success criterion is cited rather than specified locally.

R1.justification: v3 adds Bradley (2025) on learned compositional generalization and Niedoba et al. (2024) on diffusion generalization. These support the new comparison and local-denoising interpretation, while the existing related-work framework remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 adds short passages in Sections 5.2–5.3, extends Appendix H, and appends Appendix L without broadly rewriting or reorganizing the existing narrative. Local edits introduce inconsistent references such as calling Definition 5.2 and Lemma 8.1 theorems.

P2.justification: v3 adds Table 2 and Figures 16–18, comprising sample grids, score-distance plots, and score visualizations. Existing figures and Table 1 retain their content, with local caption edits and float relocations, including Figure 8 moving into the reference pages.

improvement.justification: Appendix L adds useful controlled comparisons and mechanism diagnostics. However, the new Appendix H KL derivation omits the normalization factor required by Definition 5.1, leaving the added guarantee unestablished as written; Table 2 also leaves its precise success criterion outside the supplied PDFs. These empirical benefits and new correctness and documentation concerns prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
